name: Red Hill

facts.claim: Red Hill is a rural town on the Mornington Peninsula, about 92 km from Melbourne.
Wineries have been established around Red Hill since the 1970s, taking advantage of microclimates suited to cool-climate grapes, especially pinot noir.
Strawberries, cherries and apples are grown here and sold seasonally at the farm door.
A monthly community market runs from September to May.

name: Two Bays Walking Trail

facts.claim: A 26 km hike from Dromana to Cape Schanck through Arthurs Seat State Park and Mornington Peninsula National Park.
Beyond Arthurs Seat the walk is relatively flat, through eucalypt forest and grassy Greens Bush to coastal cliffs near Cape Schanck.
It suits a two-day hike, a long day hike or section by section, and is marked with a Blue Wren symbol.

name: Coastal Walk (Mornington Peninsula)

facts.claim: A two-day walk through Mornington Peninsula National Park along high clifftops, coastal vegetation and past ocean beaches.
The national park spans the wild ocean beaches between Portsea and Flinders.

name: Bushrangers Bay

facts.claim: The Bushrangers Bay Walk starts at the eastern car park at Cape Schanck Lighthouse and drops to a sandy beach ringed by basalt cliffs, at the outlet of Main Creek.
It is a 5.4 km return walk of about 2 hours on sandy unsealed paths with steep stairs.
Rockpools can be explored at low tide, and the Main Creek estuary may need wading when the tide is in.
Swimming is not recommended: the beach is unpatrolled with rips and strong currents.

name: Arthurs Seat State Park

facts.claim: The 314 m summit gives views that on a clear day reach the Melbourne skyline, the You Yangs and Mount Macedon.
The park has walking and mountain-bike tracks, a circuit walk to Kings Falls and Seawinds Garden with William Ricketts sculptures.
The Arthurs Seat Eagle gondola, run separately, rises above the trees; the Two Bays Walking Trail passes through the park.

facts.claim: The blowhole is on the Flinders coast, viewed from a small lookout high on a headland above the rock shore.
A short steep track with many steps leads from the car park down to the shoreline and rockpools.
The blowhole is best seen working at low tide; swimming is not recommended because of rips and large waves.
